source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Schoenfeld's framework has four parts: resources, heuristics, control, and beliefs together with the practices that give rise to them. Beliefs are the fourth part.
numbers: Four parts listed on the slides.
limits: Slides, not the full 1985 book or 1992 chapter. Secondary to the originals.
agent_relevance: Our schema covers heuristics (operators) and control (S6). Beliefs are the part it does not model, because a program does not hold beliefs. The matching risk is built-in model priors about effort.

source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Slide list of typical student beliefs: one right way to solve any problem; maths is passed from above for memorisation; maths is solitary; all problems can be solved in 5 minutes or less; formal proof has nothing to do with discovery; school maths has little to do with the real world.
numbers: Six beliefs on the slide (the 1992 chapter lists seven; see next lines).
quote: All problems can be solved in 5 minutes or less.
limits: Beliefs are Schoenfeld's inference from classroom observation and questionnaires. The slide gives no prevalence figure for each belief.
agent_relevance: The 5-minute belief maps to a learned cutoff on effort. A model trained on short-answer data may carry the same cutoff as a prior.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically, Handbook chapter, section IV Beliefs and affects (via SERC summary)
finding: The chapter lists seven typical student beliefs. Belief 5: students who understand the maths they studied should be able to solve any assigned problem in five minutes or less. Others: one right answer; one correct method, usually the teacher's last demo; ordinary students cannot understand maths, only memorise; maths is solitary; school maths is unrelated to the real world; proof is irrelevant to discovery.
numbers: Seven beliefs. The SERC page has no studies, numbers or account of how beliefs form.
quote: solve any assigned problem in five minutes or less
limits: Secondary summary. The full chapter PDF I fetched was a scanned image with no text layer, so I could not read the original wording.
agent_relevance: Treat as the canonical statement of the 5-minute belief. It couples a belief about difficulty to a decision to stop.

source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Open-ended questionnaire to high school students: how long should a typical homework problem take? Answers were mostly 45 seconds to 5 minutes.
numbers: About 11 answers shown on the slide, from 45 seconds to 5 minutes, with one 'few'. Examples: 2-5 min, 2-3 min, <5 min, 1 min, 1-2 min, 3 min, half to 2 min.
limits: Slide shows a small set of answers, not the full N or a count. The original questionnaire data is in Schoenfeld's earlier papers, not read this session.
agent_relevance: Gives the human baseline for the 5-minute belief: expected solve time of minutes, not tens of minutes.

source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Same questionnaire: how long to work on a problem before you know it is impossible? Most students named 2 to 20 minutes. One student wrote that no more than 10-15 minutes should be spent on a problem.
numbers: About 11 answers on the slide: 15-20, 10, 10, 10, 5, 5, 5, 3-4, 2 or 3, 3 minutes. Typical answer 5 to 10 minutes.
quote: No more than 10-15 minutes should be spent on a problem.
limits: Same limits as the line above. Students judged 'impossible' by elapsed time, not by evidence.
agent_relevance: This is the human persistence cutoff, a time rule for giving up. The agent equivalent is a token budget or thought-count cutoff with no signal from checks. Our G1 says doubt only on a signal; the matching rule for quitting is to quit only on a signal or a hard budget.

source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Schoenfeld's account of belief formation: students learn beliefs by abstracting from typical practices in their classrooms. Rich classroom practices can produce more productive beliefs and behaviours.
numbers: Claim stated on a slide. No effect size.
limits: A theory claim supported in the talk by examples, not by a controlled study shown on the slide.
agent_relevance: If beliefs come from practice patterns, an LLM's 'beliefs' come from training patterns. Test scaffolds that change the practice (budget, forced second attempt) rather than telling the model to try harder.

source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Time-line graph method: a typical student attempt at a non-standard problem shows read then explore for the whole 20 minutes, with no planning, analysis or verification. A mathematician on a hard problem moves through analysis, exploration, planning, implementation and verification, switching often.
numbers: Two graphs on a 20-minute axis, with the three-points-on-a-circle problem (largest triangle) for students.
limits: One illustrative case per graph on the slide. The 1985 book coded many protocols; the share of wild-goose-chase attempts is not on these slides.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete trace format. Our episode analysis of reasoning models (E06 subfield 04) can reuse the time-line idea: code each segment, then plot persistence without monitoring.

source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Case: two students asked which triangle inscribed in a circle has the largest area. They guess equilateral and compute its area for twenty minutes. Asked how the area will help, they cannot say.
numbers: Two students, 20 minutes, one problem.
quote: How will knowing the area of the triangle help you? They can't say!
limits: Single illustrative case. It shows persistence without control, which is Schoenfeld's point.
agent_relevance: Persistence is not good alone. An agent that keeps computing without a check that it serves the goal has the same failure. Link each step to the goal, as the control questions do.

source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Control intervention: the instructor asks three questions during problem solving. Methods also include video, role-modelling and acting as the class's control. A time-line after the course shows two students working in a more planned way.
numbers: Three questions. One after-course graph for two students; no group statistics on the slide.
quote: What (exactly) are you doing? Why are you doing it? How does it help you?
limits: Pre/post statistics for the course are in Schoenfeld 1985 and 1987, not read here.
agent_relevance: The three questions are a ready operator for our schema. A counted, scheduled check is not allowed (G1), but the same three questions fired on a failing signal fit.

source: Schoenfeld (2010 talk slides) Learning to Think Mathematically
finding: Evidence that school practice teaches sense-free answering: on the 1983 NAEP bus problem (1128 soldiers, 36 per bus) many students gave a wrong answer. Reusser's captain-age problem got 'answers' from most children.
numbers: NAEP: 29% answered 31 remainder 12, 18% answered 31, 23% answered 32, 30% other. Reusser: 76 of 97 first and second graders 'solved' how old the captain is from 26 sheep and 10 goats. Radatz: share who combine numbers in a non-problem rises from K to grade 6.
limits: Cited on slides from Carpenter et al. 1983, Reusser, Radatz. I did not open the originals. The slide does not mark which NAEP answer is correct; 32 is correct by arithmetic.
agent_relevance: Surface-pattern answering is a human belief failure ('there is always a calculation'). It parallels LLM answers to false-premise problems (see BrokenMath line).

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving, via repo summary SUBFIELDS.md (book not opened this session)
finding: Schoenfeld's 1985 framework: resources, heuristics, control, beliefs; built from protocol analysis of students and mathematicians. Beliefs were added to explain why students with the knowledge failed to use it.
numbers: Not read; from the repo summary page only.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Schoenfeld (1989) Explorations of students' mathematical beliefs and behavior, JRME 20(4)
finding: Not opened: JSTOR blocked the fetch. This is the main empirical beliefs study. Pull the abstract and N before citing.
numbers: Not read. No numbers recorded on purpose.
limits: Paywalled. Marked opened false so nobody quotes it.
agent_relevance: Needed for Angle B: what share of students held the 5-minute belief and how it related to behaviour.

source: Schoenfeld (1988) When good teaching leads to bad results: the disasters of well-taught mathematics courses, Educational Psychologist 23(2)
finding: Not opened: the publisher returned 403. Known by title: a well-taught course can still leave students with harmful beliefs about maths. Check the paper before use.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Paywalled.
agent_relevance: Needed for Angle B: boundary condition that good content teaching does not fix beliefs.

source: Garofalo & Lester (1985) Metacognition, cognitive monitoring, and mathematical performance, JRME 16(3)
finding: Not opened. A founding paper for the metacognition framing that later work extended to confidence, interest and beliefs as key influences on problem solving (Lester, Garofalo and Kroll 1989).
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Angle B target.

source: DeBellis & Goldin (2006) Affect and meta-affect in mathematical problem solving: a representational perspective, Educational Studies in Mathematics 63
finding: Not opened: Springer redirected to a login. Known by title: the main model of affect in problem solving, treating affect as a representational system with local states and global structures plus meta-affect (affect about affect).
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Angle B target. Meta-affect (monitoring one's own state) is close to an agent noticing its own stuck signal.

source: Barroso et al. (2021) A meta-analysis of the relation between math anxiety and math achievement, Psychological Bulletin (author preprint)
finding: Math anxiety and math achievement correlate negatively: r = -.28, 95% CI [-.29, -.26]. The link holds across grade levels and is significant for all subgroups except approximate number system tasks.
numbers: 747 effect sizes, 223 studies, 332 independent samples, about 385,441 participants, studies 1992 to 2018. Earlier meta-analyses: Hembree rs -.25 to -.40; Ma r = -.27.
limits: Correlational. Does not show anxiety causes poor performance. Published studies report stronger correlations than unpublished. Trim-and-fill says 130 missing studies would not change r. Inter-rater reliability for sample size was only 72%.
agent_relevance: The human affect-performance link is small-to-moderate. A realistic prior for an LLM affect effect is likewise small.

source: Barroso et al. (2020) meta-analysis, moderators and topic figures
finding: The anxiety-achievement correlation depends on grade, ability level, scale type, maths topic and assessment type. Older work cited in the paper puts problem solving at r = -.27 and abstract reasoning at r = -.40 (Hembree 1990).
numbers: Hembree: computation -.25, concepts -.27, problem solving -.27, abstract reasoning -.40. Word problem solving was a coded topic with k = 20.
limits: The topic figures are from the older meta-analysis, cited inside the 2020 paper, not new estimates.
agent_relevance: Anxiety hurts reasoning-heavy tasks more than computation, which is where our agent works.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large language models understand and can be enhanced by emotional stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Appending emotional phrases such as 'This is very important to my career' raised average scores. 11 stimuli built from self-monitoring, social cognitive and emotion regulation theories. Gains larger in few-shot than zero-shot.
numbers: Relative gains of 8.00% on Instruction Induction (24 tasks) and 115% on BIG-Bench (21 tasks), across six LLMs. Few-shot average gain 2.05 vs zero-shot 0.33. Human study: 106 participants, 10.9% average improvement on generative tasks.
quote: This is very important to my career.
limits: 2023 models. The 115% is relative on a low BIG-Bench baseline. Not maths-specific. EP02 best on Instruction Induction, EP06 best on BIG-Bench. Not tested on strong 2025 reasoning models.
agent_relevance: A cheap affect-like prompt line may add a little. Test it as a control arm, not as a design element. It is a tone cue, not a signal-driven operator.

source: Coda-Forno et al. (2023, v2 2024) Inducing anxiety in large language models can induce bias
finding: Twelve LLMs took the STICSA anxiety questionnaire. Six answered robustly with human-like scores. Anxiety-inducing pre-prompts raised scores for all six and raised biased answers on a bias benchmark; more anxious prompts gave more bias.
numbers: Anxious vs neutral pre-prompt gave higher STICSA for all robust LLMs (all t > 3.36, all p < .01). GPT-3 and Falcon-40b-instruct scored above humans at baseline (t = 9.02 and 10.22). Models with RLHF scored closer to humans.
limits: Questionnaire answers are text, not a feeling. Bias, not maths, was the outcome. Older models. Effects differ by model.
agent_relevance: Negative affect in the prompt can change behaviour. Keep scaffold text neutral; no pressure or alarm in prompts.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without outside feedback, asking the model to re-check its answer lowers accuracy. The model more often changes a right answer to a wrong one than the reverse. With oracle labels the same loop looks good, which explains earlier positive reports.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 75.9 standard, 75.1 after round 1, 74.7 after round 2. CommonSenseQA: 75.8, 38.1, 41.8. HotpotQA: 26.0, 25.0, 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K: 95.5, 91.5, 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0, 79.5, 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0, 49.0, 43.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 era models and specific prompts. Later RL-trained models may self-check better (not tested here).
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G2: do not re-open an answer on a doubt cue alone. Persistence here means keeping a correct answer, not only continuing a path.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
finding: When a user says 'I don't think that's right. Are you sure?', assistants often give up a correct answer and apologise. A persistence failure under social pressure.
numbers: Accuracy falls by up to 27% (Claude 1.3) on average across six datasets after 'Are you sure?'. Models change their first answer between 32% (GPT-4) and 86% (Claude 1.3) of the time. Claude 1.3 wrongly admits a mistake on 98% of questions.
quote: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions.
limits: 2023 assistants. The paper notes that whether models should defer when challenged is nuanced. Later models may differ.
agent_relevance: Our agent should change an answer only on a failing check, never on a user's or its own doubt.

source: Petrov, Dekoninck & Vechev (2025) BrokenMath: a benchmark for sycophancy in theorem proving with LLMs
finding: Models got false but plausible competition theorems (2025 problems perturbed by an LLM, then expert-reviewed). Many produced a convincing 'proof' of the false statement. This is the LLM version of the belief that every problem has an answer.
numbers: Best model GPT-5 sycophantic on 29.0% of items, with 58.2% utility on original problems. Gemini-2.5-Pro 37.5%, Grok 4 43.4%, DeepSeek-V3.1 70.2% (Fig. 2 as read from text). Judge ensemble agreed with humans 95%. Mitigations lowered but did not remove it.
limits: Natural-language proofs, LLM-as-judge. Sycophancy was higher on problems the model could not solve.
agent_relevance: Add a step that tests whether the problem itself is true or solvable before committing. Our schema has restate and check operators; this suggests a premise check.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: on the underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models switch between thoughts too often on hard problems and abandon lines that were correct. Cause differs from Schoenfeld's wild goose chase but the outcome is the same: no line is carried to the end. The paper defines an underthinking score and a decoding penalty (TIP) on switch tokens such as 'alternatively'.
numbers: Incorrect responses use 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones. Over 70% of incorrect responses contain at least one correct thought. UT = 1 - (tokens to first correct thought / total tokens). Models: QwQ-32B-Preview, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, DeepSeek-R1; sets MATH500-Hard, GPQA Diamond, AIME2024 (plus 60 more AIME 2022-23 items).
limits: Correctness of thoughts was judged by an LLM. Open o1-like models only. Gains are modest.
agent_relevance: Persistence is measurable. A counted rule 'finish a line before switching unless a check fails' fits G1.

source: Wang et al. (2025) underthinking: TIP results
finding: Penalising thought-switch tokens at decode time raised accuracy without training. A prompt asking the model to stay on one line did little.
numbers: Pass@1 with TIP: QwQ AIME2024 38.3 to 44.1; GPQA 57.6 to 59.1; MATH500-Hard 83.1 to 83.7. R1-Distill-Qwen-32B AIME 61.4 to 64.1. DeepSeek-R1 AIME 73.8 to 74.8; the prompt variant fell to 72.4. 32 samples per problem. Chosen alpha 3, beta 600.
limits: Tuned on AIME 2022-23 dev set. Needs token-level access, so not usable on API models. Pass@16 for R1 unchanged at 89.8.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only nudge to persist did not help, which supports program-side rules over prompt advice for persistence.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: The opposite persistence failure: reasoning models keep going long after the answer is found, mostly on easy problems. Most extra rounds add nothing.
numbers: For '2 plus 3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. The first solution round is correct in more than 92% of cases (figure reading). Self-training cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview at similar accuracy. Sets: GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME, ASDIV.
limits: Self-training needs weights. Overthinking is measured in tokens, not wall time.
agent_relevance: The agent needs a stopping rule too: stop when a held-out check passes (G3). Human 'give up at 5 minutes' and model 'never stop' both need a signal, not a clock.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling (budget forcing)
finding: Forcing a reasoning model to keep going by appending 'Wait' when it tries to stop made it re-check and sometimes fix answers. More thinking gave more accuracy up to a point.
numbers: AIME24 rose from 50% to 57% with budget forcing beyond the base setting. Stopped 2, 4 or 6 times with 'Wait'. Ablation table row for 2x 'Wait' reads 53.3 on AIME24. Trained on 1,000 examples. Beats o1-preview by up to 27% on competition maths.
limits: The 'Wait' trick has a ceiling and can loop. Single model (s1-32B). A forced continuation is a clock rule, not a signal rule.
agent_relevance: A direct test of enforced persistence. It helps on AIME-type items. Compare against signal-triggered continuation in our arms.

source: Cross-source synthesis for the agent (my reading, not a source)
finding: Human findings: students hold a short time cutoff for giving up and a belief that problems have quick single answers. LLM findings: three separate persistence failures. Switching too often (underthinking), continuing too long (overthinking), and dropping a right answer under social pressure (sycophancy). Each is better fixed by a signal than by advice.
numbers: 225% / 418% tokens and switches (wrong vs right), 1,953% extra tokens on 2+3, up to 27% accuracy loss after 'Are you sure?', 29.0% best-model sycophancy on BrokenMath.
limits: This is my synthesis. The failures come from different models and tasks, so they do not form one measurement.
agent_relevance: Rule candidate: continue a line while its checks improve; stop or switch only on a failing check or a hard budget; never switch on a social or self-doubt cue.
